caption:
Braised Beef Wonton Noodle Soup, Sang Kee Restaurant @sangkeechinatown,  Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. 

Sang Kee has been a beloved institution in Philadelphia’s Chinatown for decades, and its popularity is rooted in a few key factors. The restaurant is most famous for its Peking Duck, a signature dish it introduced to the city in 1980. People come from all over for the perfectly crispy skin and tender meat of this dish.

Beyond the duck, Sang Kee is renowned for its authentic Hong Kong-style and Cantonese cuisine. The restaurant has built a reputation for offering high-quality food with generous portions at a reasonable price. This combination of delicious, traditional dishes and great value has made it a favorite spot for everything from family gatherings to quick, casual meals.

If you haven’t been to Apricot Stone in Northern Liberties yet… you are seriously missing out 😍 Hands down the best Armenian food in Philly. 🇦🇲♥️

Ara, the owner, is the friendliest guy ever, and his mom — who’s been a professional chef since 1991 — is also in the kitchen. They’ve been running Apricot Stone for about nine and a half years now, and it truly feels like a family-run gem.

My bestie and I went for their $100 Date Night Menu (BYOB 🍷 & such a good deal), and honestly it felt like we were back at Armenian sleepaway camp. The flavors were so authentic. Just like something our grandmothers would have made and every bite brought back memories. 🥹

The spread was incredible: apps, entrees, sides… everything was to die for and the portions were so generous. A few of my go-to favorites are the manti, shrimp saganaki, and lamajun. All perfectly made. For the $100 dinner for 2, we got the dip trio (our faves: red pepper feta, tabouleh & lebni), stuffed grape leaves, cheese boreg, spanakopita, and falafel.

For mains, the dinner also comes with an entree-sized salad; we chose the Fattoush salad (so fun, it comes with a little mallet to crack the pita shell!) plus the lamb skewer and luleh skewer, both cooked to perfection. And of course, dessert was the cherry on top: their decadent house-made Dubai chocolate (to die for). I also highly recommend my absolute favorite, the Khataif. 🤤

They’re also open for lunch and have a private party space upstairs.

Apricot Stone is one of those rare restaurants that feels like home while also being one of the most delicious meals you’ll ever have in the city. Can’t recommend it enough!

Cuisine: Mediterranean (Syrian and Armenian)

Rating: 3.5/5

Price: $$

Review & Recommendations:
Apricot Stone is a restaurant off of Girard Ave serving traditional Armenian and Syrian food. In addition to a wide range of vegetarian options available, they also have a monthly special menu that expands to incorporate seasonal ingredients. Their April menu had refreshing and unique dishes like the Eggplant Fatteh which resembled Indian street chat in a lot of ways. The table favorite was, however, the Mujaddara- a rather simple dish made from lentils and sweetened by caramelized onions that felt like a warm hug from the first bite. A fun play of flavors and textures, our first experience of Armenian food was definitely quite interesting. Overall, while it might take some time for our pallet to favor these flavors, if you want to try a different cuisine too, Apricot Stone is surely a safe bet to place.

Went to @ApricotStonePhilly for a family dinner. It was my first time. The chef, Chef Fimy, hails from Alleppo and creates a fusion of Syrian and Armenian heritage. This was followed by falafel, pita, manti Armenian open faced dumplings, cheese boreg and spanakopita. We then had the luleh, lamb, filet, and chicken kabobs served with pilaf. We ended with healthy servings of baklava, gatnabur (an Armenian rice pudding) and khataif (shredded dough with cream & cheese, served hot). It’s a small restaurant (426 Girard Ave, Philadelphia) with a big heart and we certainly ate more that we should have. Recommend!!

This week’s restaurant was a Taiwanese and Szechuan kitchen- Dan Dan, located close to the Rittenhouse Square. Out-of-the-Pot Chicken & Herb Broth

A cherished classic from the Swargalok district of Sukhothai. An aromatic and uniquely delicious broth, unlike any other curry. Its unique name matches its distinctive preparation: chicken is first simmered in coconut milk, then     finished "out of the pot" with a bounty of fresh herbs and vegetables, banana blossom, cilantro, scallion, lemongrass and Northern style Lab paste.

Historically influenced by contact with European seafarers, this unique curry is a testament to Ayutthaya's role as a global trading hub. Yam Kai Yang Tao
Chicken Salad
Chicken, coconut milk, roasted chili paste, lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, galangal, ginger, boiled eggs, chilies, mint. A royal Thai dish with a fascinating history—originally prepared with turtle meat (a rare tribute ingredient), it was later adapted with chicken due to scarcity and conservation. 
*Princess Vimaddha masterfully crafted this salad to balance the meat’s bold aroma by simmering it in coconut milk, then blending it with roasted chili paste, lemongrass, and fragrant herbs for a subtly sweet, aromatic taste. Its exquisite flavor won the admiration of King Rama V, securing its legacy in Thai cuisine.Served with fresh vegetables.

ก๋วยเตี๊ยวเรือรังสิต (Rangsit Thai Boat Noodles Soup)**  
**A Taste of Thai History**  
This dish has its roots in the bustling canals of Thailand, where it was originally served from boats by vendors. The rich, flavorful broth and hearty ingredients made it a favorite among workers and locals alike. Today, it’s a beloved classic that represents the ingenuity and resourcefulness of Thai cuisine. 

**What’s in the Bowl?**  
- **Rich, aromatic broth**: Slow-cooked to perfection with a blend of spices and herbs.  
- **Choice of protein**: Tender beef or succulent pork.  
- **Rice noodles**: Soft and chewy, perfect for soaking up the flavorful broth.  
- **Toppings**: Bean sprouts, Thai basil, and crispy fried garlic for added texture and flavor.  

**Why You’ll Love It:**

Khao Soi Chiang Mai | $20
“This dish traces its roots back to Yunnan, China, and traveled along the ancient Silk Road through Burma before arriving in Northern Thailand. Over time, it evolved into a distinct Northern Thai dish, combining local ingredients and flavors to create a unique culinary experience. Today, Khao Soi is a globally recognized dish that represents the rich culinary heritage of Chiang Mai.
Khao Soi features a slow-cooked curry coconut broth that is rich and aromatic, layered with complex spices and herbs. This dish is served with egg noodles, both soft and crispy, adding texture to the meal. Traditional accompaniments include pickled mustard greens, dried shallots and house-made chili paste for an extra kick of flavor.“
